headline: RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro launches with a removable action cam, waterproof to 5 meters
summary: The RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro features a magnetic, removable action camera that records 2.7K video and is waterproof to 5m. The phone itself boasts IP68/IP69K durability and a 120Hz display.
details: RugOne, part of Ulefon, has unveiled its new Xsnap 7 Pro rugged smartphone at IFA 2026. This device stands out with a magnetic removable camera unit that functions as an action cam, capable of recording video up to 2.7K resolution at 30fps and includes 64GB of built-in storage.

The almost cube-shaped camera module weighs 39 grams and can run for up to 40 minutes on a full charge. It broadcasts a preview feed to RugOne's companion app up to 50 meters away, and includes software features like distortion correction, horizon lock, and Freeframe shooting mode.

This action cam is waterproof up to five meters without additional cases. RugOne will also include a companion magnet pendant for body-worn capture, and it is compatible with third-party accessories supporting a universal mount.

Beyond the action cam, the Xsnap 7 Pro features a 50-megapixel "AI main camera" with optical image stabilization. It also includes a 64MP infrared night-vision camera with IR LEDs, designed for crisp black-and-white detail in low-light conditions.

The phone itself sports a 6.67-inch display with 1,700-nit peak brightness and up to 120Hz refresh rates. Powered by a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor, it boasts strong durability with IP68 and IP69K ratings, handling water submersion up to two meters for 30 minutes and 1.5-meter drops onto concrete.

Officially debuting at IFA, early-bird sales for the Xsnap 7 Pro open on Kickstarter on September 7 at a discounted preorder price of 799 euros (roughly $930). Global sales will follow next month on Amazon and RugOne's online store, priced at $999, available in Sand Dune and Classic Black.

headline_marked: [[Prompting is evolving]] into 'Graph Engineering' for advanced AI agents
headline: Prompting is evolving into 'Graph Engineering' for advanced AI agents
summary: The viral term 'Graph Engineering' describes breaking down AI agent tasks into smaller, interconnected nodes, a refinement of existing orchestration methods like LangGraph, not a complete replacement for prompting.
details: Despite recent claims on social media that 'prompting will be dead in six months,' experts suggest that AI prompting is not dying but rather evolving into more sophisticated forms like 'Graph Engineering.' This new approach refines how AI agents tackle complex tasks.

Traditionally, an AI agent might loop through an entire task by itself until it deems the output sufficient. This monolithic approach can be inefficient and prone to errors, as the model has to manage all aspects of a task simultaneously.

Graph Engineering breaks down complex AI tasks into smaller, specialized units called nodes. Each node is assigned a specific job, such as being a researcher, a writer, or a fact-checker, and can even have its own dedicated model call or agent.

Nodes are interconnected by 'edges,' which determine the workflow based on the output of the preceding node. For example, if a fact-checker node identifies an error, the edge can send the task back to the writer node with specific feedback for correction, ensuring quality control before progression.

This concept is not entirely new; it's an evolution of orchestration techniques developers have used for over a year with tools like LangGraph. The recent viral spread of the term 'Graph Engineering' simply highlights a refined approach to existing methodologies.

The terminology for these advanced prompting and orchestration methods frequently changes, from 'loop engineering' to 'harness engineering' and 'context engineering.' Each new term often signifies a slight improvement or a new perspective on the same underlying idea.

What is truly becoming obsolete is the simplistic idea of creating a finished agentic system by merely combining one model with a single, clever prompt. The future lies in structured, multi-step processes that allow for more robust and reliable AI agent performance.
